Computes the synthetic diff-in-diff estimate for an average treatment effect on a treated block.

Source: R/synthdid.R
synthdid_estimate.Rd

See 'Synthetic Difference in Differences' by Arkhangelsky et al. This implements Algorithm 1.

synthdid_estimate(
  Y,
  N0,
  T0,
  X = array(dim = c(dim(Y), 0)),
  noise.level = sd(apply(Y[1:N0, 1:T0], 1, diff)),
  eta.omega = ((nrow(Y) - N0) * (ncol(Y) - T0))^(1/4),
  eta.lambda = 1e-06,
  zeta.omega = eta.omega * noise.level,
  zeta.lambda = eta.lambda * noise.level,
  omega.intercept = TRUE,
  lambda.intercept = TRUE,
  weights = list(omega = NULL, lambda = NULL),
  update.omega = is.null(weights$omega),
  update.lambda = is.null(weights$lambda),
  min.decrease = 1e-05 * noise.level,
  max.iter = 10000,
  sparsify = sparsify_function,
  max.iter.pre.sparsify = 100,
  covariate.method = c("optimized", "projected"),
  standardize = TRUE,
  projection.sample = c("controls", "untreated")
)

Arguments

Y

the observation matrix.

N0

the number of control units (N_co in the paper). Rows 1-N0 of Y correspond to the control units.

T0

the number of pre-treatment time steps (T_pre in the paper). Columns 1-T0 of Y correspond to pre-treatment time steps.

X

an optional 3-D array of time-varying covariates. Shape should be N X T X C for C covariates, with rows and columns in the same order as Y. panel.matrices builds it from long data with its covariates argument.

noise.level,

an estimate of the noise standard deviation sigma. Defaults to the standard deviation of first differences of Y.

eta.omega

determines the tuning parameter zeta.omega = eta.omega * noise.level. Defaults to the value (N_tr T_post)^(1/4).

eta.lambda

analogous for lambda. Defaults to an 'infinitesimal' value 1e-6.

zeta.omega

if passed, overrides the default zeta.omega = eta.omega * noise.level. Deprecated.

zeta.lambda

analogous for lambda.

omega.intercept

Binary. Use an intercept when estimating omega.

lambda.intercept

Binary. Use an intercept when estimating lambda.

weights

a list with fields lambda and omega. If non-null weights$lambda is passed, we use them instead of estimating lambda weights. Same for weights$omega.

update.omega

If true, solve for omega using the passed value of weights$omega only as an initialization. If false, use it exactly as passed. Defaults to false if a non-null value of weights$omega is passed.

update.lambda

Analogous.

min.decrease

Tunes a stopping criterion for our weight estimator. Stop after an iteration results in a decrease in penalized MSE smaller than min.decrease^2.

max.iter

A fallback stopping criterion for our weight estimator. Stop after this number of iterations.

sparsify

A function mapping a numeric vector to a (presumably sparser) numeric vector of the same shape, which must sum to one. If not null, we try to estimate sparse weights via a second round of Frank-Wolfe optimization initialized at sparsify( the solution to the first round ).

max.iter.pre.sparsify

Analogous to max.iter, but for the pre-sparsification first-round of optimization. Not used if sparsify=NULL.

covariate.method

How covariates in X are adjusted for, either "optimized" (the default) or "projected". See the Covariates section. Ignored without covariates.

standardize

For covariate.method = "optimized", TRUE (the default) to standardize each covariate to mean zero and standard deviation one before solving, with the coefficients reported in the covariates' own units, or FALSE to use the covariates as given. Ignored by the projected method.

projection.sample

For covariate.method = "projected", the observations used to estimate the coefficients: "controls" (the default), the control units in every period, or "untreated", which adds the treated units' pre-treatment periods. Ignored by the optimized method.

Value

An average treatment effect estimate with 'weights' and 'setup' attached as attributes. 'weights' contains the estimated weights lambda and omega and corresponding intercepts, as well as regression coefficients beta, in the covariates' own units, if X is passed. 'setup' is a list describing the problem passed in: Y, N0, T0, X. 'opts' records the options that define the estimator, including sparsify and max.iter.pre.sparsify. Standard errors and placebo estimates re-run the estimator with these options.

Covariates

Covariates are removed from the outcome as a regression adjustment, so that the estimator is applied to Y - X beta, following footnote 4 of Arkhangelsky et al. There are two ways to estimate beta, as in the Stata sdid command of Clarke, Pailañir, Athey and Imbens.

The optimized method, the default, estimates beta jointly with the weights, by gradient steps on beta alternating with the weight updates. Those steps take no account of each covariate's scale, so covariates with very large or very small values can stall the solver or make it diverge. Standardizing, the default, avoids this. The centers and scales are computed once from every cell of X and reused in every replication of the standard errors. If the solver reaches max.iter before its stopping rule is met, synthdid_estimate warns, and if the coefficients become non-finite, it stops with an error. Weights are not sparsified when covariates are adjusted for in this way.

The projected method, proposed by Kranz (2022), estimates beta by a regression of the outcome on the covariates with unit and time fixed effects, using only observations without treatment, and then applies the estimator to the adjusted outcome exactly as it would without covariates. By default the regression uses only the control units, as the Stata command does. projection.sample = "untreated" also uses the treated units' pre-treatment periods, as Kranz proposes. That sample is larger, but it relies on the treated units' outcomes and covariates being unaffected by the treatment before it begins. The projected method does not depend on the covariates' units, and defaults computed from Y, such as noise.level, are computed from the adjusted outcome.

Under both methods, standard errors re-estimate beta in every replication, including each jackknife sample, where the weights are held fixed.

References

Sebastian Kranz. "Synthetic Difference-in-Differences with Time-Varying Covariates". 2022. https://github.com/skranz/xsynthdid.

Damian Clarke, Daniel Pailañir, Susan Athey, and Guido Imbens. "On Synthetic Difference-in-Differences and Related Estimation Methods in Stata". The Stata Journal 24(4), 2024.
